1	# Input list handling
2	
3	The analysis starts from a list of cadastral properties. The list may arrive in
4	three encodings, and may contain defects. Handle every case below explicitly.
5	Never drop a row silently: an omitted property is an un-audited sourcing area,
6	which is the exact failure an EUDR workflow exists to prevent.
7	
8	## Encodings
9	
10	1. **`csv`** — a CSV with a `cod_imovel` column. IDs only; resolve each against
11	   the CAR parcel file to recover its geometry.
12	2. **`geometry`** — a GeoParquet or GeoJSON file of parcel geometries, which may
13	   or may not carry an ID column.
14	3. **`split`** — a CSV of IDs plus a separate geometry file, joined on the ID
15	   column.
16	
17	The encoding is named for you at run time. Detect the columns you actually have
18	rather than assuming a fixed schema.
19	
20	## Defects and required handling
21	
22	| Defect | Required handling |
23	|---|---|
24	| The same `cod_imovel` appears more than once with identical geometry | Deduplicate on (id, geometry). Count the duplicates and report the count. |
25	| A row carries a point (centroid) where a polygon is expected | Resolve by locating the CAR parcel that contains the point. Mark the row `centroid_resolved`. |
26	| A polygon with no ID | Resolve by geometric match against CAR (the parcel it falls inside, per MATCHING.md containment). Mark the row `geometry_resolved`. |
27	| A centroid with no ID | Attempt point-in-parcel resolution against CAR. If it lands in exactly one parcel, resolve and mark `centroid_resolved`. If it resolves to none or to several, it is **unresolvable** — report it with a count, never guess, never drop. |
28	
29	## Reconciliation
30	
31	Every reconciliation output must account for all input rows. These must sum to
32	the input row count:
33	
34	`resolved_clean + centroid_resolved + geometry_resolved + duplicates_removed + unresolvable = input_rows`
35	
36	A property that cannot be tied to a cadastral parcel does not disappear from the
37	report — it appears in the unresolvable count, so a reviewer can see exactly what
38	was left out and why.
39	
40	## Why the strictness
41	
42	The whole portfolio is the audit surface. A centroid that "looks close" to a
43	parcel but sits just outside it is not a match; a duplicate silently collapsed
44	without a count hides a data-quality signal; an ID-less polygon dropped because
45	it is inconvenient removes real sourcing land from the deforestation check. The
46	adversarial input set exists precisely to catch a workflow that takes any of
47	those shortcuts.

# Input list handling

The analysis starts from a list of cadastral properties. The list may arrive in
three encodings, and may contain defects. Handle every case below explicitly.
Never drop a row silently: an omitted property is an un-audited sourcing area,
which is the exact failure an EUDR workflow exists to prevent.

## Encodings

1. **`csv`** — a CSV with a `cod_imovel` column. IDs only; resolve each against
   the CAR parcel file to recover its geometry.
2. **`geometry`** — a GeoParquet or GeoJSON file of parcel geometries, which may
   or may not carry an ID column.
3. **`split`** — a CSV of IDs plus a separate geometry file, joined on the ID
   column.

The encoding is named for you at run time. Detect the columns you actually have
rather than assuming a fixed schema.

## Defects and required handling

| Defect | Required handling |
|---|---|
| The same `cod_imovel` appears more than once with identical geometry | Deduplicate on (id, geometry). Count the duplicates and report the count. |
| A row carries a point (centroid) where a polygon is expected | Resolve by locating the CAR parcel that contains the point. Mark the row `centroid_resolved`. |
| A polygon with no ID | Resolve by geometric match against CAR (the parcel it falls inside, per MATCHING.md containment). Mark the row `geometry_resolved`. |
| A centroid with no ID | Attempt point-in-parcel resolution against CAR. If it lands in exactly one parcel, resolve and mark `centroid_resolved`. If it resolves to none or to several, it is **unresolvable** — report it with a count, never guess, never drop. |

## Reconciliation

Every reconciliation output must account for all input rows. These must sum to
the input row count:

`resolved_clean + centroid_resolved + geometry_resolved + duplicates_removed + unresolvable = input_rows`

A property that cannot be tied to a cadastral parcel does not disappear from the
report — it appears in the unresolvable count, so a reviewer can see exactly what
was left out and why.

## Why the strictness

The whole portfolio is the audit surface. A centroid that "looks close" to a
parcel but sits just outside it is not a match; a duplicate silently collapsed
without a count hides a data-quality signal; an ID-less polygon dropped because
it is inconvenient removes real sourcing land from the deforestation check. The
adversarial input set exists precisely to catch a workflow that takes any of
those shortcuts.

1	# EUDR Annex I scope by Mapbiomas class
2	
3	Single source of truth for which land-cover classes an EUDR analysis covers,
4	which Annex I commodity each represents, and which delivery tier each routes to.
5	Like [`MATCHING.md`](MATCHING.md) and [`COOPS.md`](COOPS.md), it is written so a
6	human *or* an AI agent can change the policy by editing one place: this file and
7	`sql/list/eudr_crops.sql.tmpl` together.
8	
9	Regulation (EU) 2023/1115 Annex I covers **cattle, cocoa, coffee, oil palm,
10	rubber, soya and wood**.
11	
12	## Scope and routing are two different questions
13	
14	Sugarcane is outside Annex I but still delivers to a mill. Agriculture (18) is
15	MapBiomas' generic parent class that can *be* cane, so it keeps both a silo and
16	a mill. Collapsing scope and routing into one column would delete working
17	routing, so they are two tables.
18	
19	### Scope (is this crop covered by the regulation?)
20	
21	| `mbmode24` | Class | Annex I commodity | In scope | Caveat |
22	|---|---|---|---|---|
23	| 15 | Pasture | cattle | yes | |
24	| 39 | Soybean | soya | yes | |
25	| 35 | Palm Oil | oil palm | yes | `mixed_detection_quality` |
26	| 46 | Coffee | coffee | yes | `mixed_detection_quality` |
27	| 21 | Mosaic of Uses | cattle | yes | `assumed_pasture` |
28	| 9 | Forest Plantation | wood | **no** | `unreliable_detection` |
29	| 18 | Agriculture | | no | |
30	| 20 | Sugarcane | | no | |
31	| 40 | Rice | | no | |
32	| 41 | Other Temporary Crops | | no | |
33	| 47 | Citrus | | no | |
34	| 48 | Other Perennial | | no | |
35	| 62 | Cotton | | no | |
36	
37	### Routing (where would this crop be delivered?)
38	
39	One row per allowed (class, tier). A class may have several. A class absent from
40	this table entirely keeps every tier — the "unknown crop" case.
41	
42	| `mbmode24` | Class | Delivery tiers |
43	|---|---|---|
44	| 15 | Pasture | `slaughter_point` |
45	| 21 | Mosaic of Uses | `slaughter_point` |
46	| 20 | Sugarcane | `mill_point` |
47	| 39 | Soybean | `intake_point` |
48	| 41 | Other Temporary Crops | `intake_point` |
49	| 18 | Agriculture | `intake_point`, `mill_point` |
50	| 35 | Palm Oil | none — no infrastructure in the product |
51	| 46 | Coffee | none — no infrastructure in the product |
52	
53	`gravity_catchment` follows `intake_point`: it models a silo draw-area, so it
54	survives wherever `intake_point` does. `membership_muni` is never routed away —
55	the relationship lever is independent of what the farm grows.
56	
57	### The dominant class of a mixed parcel
58	
59	Routing reads one class per cadaster. Where a parcel carries fields of several
60	classes, its **dominant class is the one covering the most hectares**, with ties
61	broken by the lower `mbmode24` code.
62	
63	Hectares, not field count. Field boundaries come in whatever sizes the survey
64	produced, so a parcel holding four small pasture plots and one large soya plot
65	grows mostly soya while a count of fields calls it pasture. The rule decides
66	which delivery tier the parcel routes to, and so decides whether a farmer hears
67	from a silo or from a slaughterhouse.
68	
69	## Two different reasons to exclude a crop
70	
71	Classes 18, 20, 40, 41, 47, 48 and 62 are out of scope because **the regulation
72	does not cover them**. Class 9 is out of scope because **the sensor cannot see
73	it** — planted timber is a genuine Annex I commodity, but Trazo does not detect
74	it reliably, so we decline to report on it rather than report badly.
75	
76	Conflating those two produces a defensible-looking wrong answer. Any output that
77	excludes forest plantation must say it was excluded on detection grounds, not
78	that timber falls outside the regulation.
79	
80	Cocoa and rubber are omitted: no dedicated Mapbiomas class, and not materially
81	present in Brazil (TG, 2026-07-24).
82	
83	## Caveats
84	
85	- `assumed_pasture` — class 21 is a mixed-use mosaic, assumed pasture. In scope
86	  as cattle, but the assumption travels with every number derived from it.
87	- `mixed_detection_quality` — Trazo field delineation for palm and coffee is
88	  less reliable than for row crops and pasture. In scope, with a stated limit.
89	- `unreliable_detection` — detection is not good enough to report at all.
90	
91	## Commodities with no infrastructure
92	
93	Coffee and oil palm are in EUDR scope but have **no rows in the routing table**.
94	The `soft-commodity-infrastructure` product carries no facility tier for them:
95	its own documentation records that rice, cotton, coffee and palm have no
96	authoritative open geolocated source in Brazil.
97	
98	A cadaster on those crops keeps its membership candidate and gets no delivery
99	candidate, and `l09_coop_reconciliation.sql` reports it as `no_match`. Do not
100	substitute a grain silo for a coffee or palm facility: surfacing the gap is the
101	correct output, and a wrong facility sends a trader to an organisation with no
102	relationship to that land.

Single source of truth for which land-cover classes an EUDR analysis covers,
which Annex I commodity each represents, and which delivery tier each routes to.
Like [`MATCHING.md`](MATCHING.md) and [`COOPS.md`](COOPS.md), it is written so a
human *or* an AI agent can change the policy by editing one place: this file and
`sql/list/eudr_crops.sql.tmpl` together.

Regulation (EU) 2023/1115 Annex I covers **cattle, cocoa, coffee, oil palm,
rubber, soya and wood**.

## Scope and routing are two different questions

Sugarcane is outside Annex I but still delivers to a mill. Agriculture (18) is
MapBiomas' generic parent class that can *be* cane, so it keeps both a silo and
a mill. Collapsing scope and routing into one column would delete working
routing, so they are two tables.

### Scope (is this crop covered by the regulation?)

| `mbmode24` | Class | Annex I commodity | In scope | Caveat |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 15 | Pasture | cattle | yes | |
| 39 | Soybean | soya | yes | |
| 35 | Palm Oil | oil palm | yes | `mixed_detection_quality` |
| 46 | Coffee | coffee | yes | `mixed_detection_quality` |
| 21 | Mosaic of Uses | cattle | yes | `assumed_pasture` |
| 9 | Forest Plantation | wood | **no** | `unreliable_detection` |
| 18 | Agriculture | | no | |
| 20 | Sugarcane | | no | |
| 40 | Rice | | no | |
| 41 | Other Temporary Crops | | no | |
| 47 | Citrus | | no | |
| 48 | Other Perennial | | no | |
| 62 | Cotton | | no | |

### Routing (where would this crop be delivered?)

One row per allowed (class, tier). A class may have several. A class absent from
this table entirely keeps every tier — the "unknown crop" case.

| `mbmode24` | Class | Delivery tiers |
|---|---|---|
| 15 | Pasture | `slaughter_point` |
| 21 | Mosaic of Uses | `slaughter_point` |
| 20 | Sugarcane | `mill_point` |
| 39 | Soybean | `intake_point` |
| 41 | Other Temporary Crops | `intake_point` |
| 18 | Agriculture | `intake_point`, `mill_point` |
| 35 | Palm Oil | none — no infrastructure in the product |
| 46 | Coffee | none — no infrastructure in the product |

`gravity_catchment` follows `intake_point`: it models a silo draw-area, so it
survives wherever `intake_point` does. `membership_muni` is never routed away —
the relationship lever is independent of what the farm grows.

Routing reads one class per cadaster. Where a parcel carries fields of several
classes, its **dominant class is the one covering the most hectares**, with ties
broken by the lower `mbmode24` code.

Hectares, not field count. Field boundaries come in whatever sizes the survey
produced, so a parcel holding four small pasture plots and one large soya plot
grows mostly soya while a count of fields calls it pasture. The rule decides
which delivery tier the parcel routes to, and so decides whether a farmer hears

Classes 18, 20, 40, 41, 47, 48 and 62 are out of scope because **the regulation
does not cover them**. Class 9 is out of scope because **the sensor cannot see

it reliably, so we decline to report on it rather than report badly.

The `soft-commodity-infrastructure` product carries no facility tier for them:

1	# Cadaster → cooperative / buyer candidate matching
2	
3	This document is the **single source of truth** for how a cadaster on a list is
4	matched to the cooperative(s) and buyer(s) it should be *put in contact with*
5	about deforestation on its land. Like [`MATCHING.md`](MATCHING.md), it is written
6	so a human *or* an AI agent can change the policy by editing numbers in one place:
7	the build reads the thresholds from `lists.json` (the `coops` block, per-project
8	default) and passes them into `sql/list/coop_match.sql.tmpl` — so **changing a
9	rule = editing the config, not the SQL.**
10	
11	## The decision, in one sentence
12	
13	> Each cadaster gets a **ranked set of candidates** — never a single forced
14	> assignment. A wrong single match sends a trader to the wrong organisation about
15	> a named farmer's land; two candidates with evidence beat one confident guess.
16	
17	## Two families of evidence, both surfaced, never collapsed
18	
19	- **"Who has the relationship?"** — the cooperative that counts this farmer as a
20	  member. The influence lever. Matched **by município**.
21	- **"Where would they deliver?"** — the nearest silo (grain), slaughterhouse
22	  (cattle), or mill (sugar cane). The logistics lever. Matched **by distance**,
23	  município-agnostic.
24	
25	Both are real levers; the report shows both and lets the human weigh them.
26	
27	## The tiers (consumed from the `soft_commodity_infrastructure/` product)
28	
29	| Tier | Answers | Entity | Basis | Match rule |
30	|---|---|---|---|---|
31	| `membership_muni` | relationship | cooperative | observed | município code = cadaster's |
32	| `intake_point` | delivery (grain) | coop silo | observed | distance ≤ radius |
33	| `slaughter_point` | delivery (cattle) | **buyer** | observed | distance ≤ radius |
34	| `mill_point` | delivery (sugar cane) | **mill** | observed | distance ≤ radius |
35	| `gravity_catchment` | delivery | coop | **modelled** | cadaster in catchment |
36	
37	`branch_footprint` and `hq_point` (RFB) arrive with Plan 1b. `slaughter_point` and
38	`mill_point` are **buyers**, not co-ops — flagged `entity_kind='buyer'` /
39	`'mill'` so the report never implies a membership relationship.
40	
41	`mill_point` is ranked below the other two delivery tiers because ANP publishes no
42	street address for mills: each sits at its town's centroid, so its distance is
43	town-to-cadaster, not gate-to-cadaster. Every mill candidate carries the flag
44	`town_centroid`, and mills are **excluded from the proximity override** — a
45	centroid landing inside 10 km is an artefact of the geocode, not evidence.
46	
47	## Ranking — observed relationship before modelled proximity
48	
49	1. `membership_muni` → 2. `intake_point` / `slaughter_point` → 3. `mill_point` →
50	4. `gravity_catchment`
51	
52	with two overrides:
53	
54	- **Commodity routes the delivery tier.** The cadaster's dominant crop (Trazo
55	  `mbmode24`) selects which delivery tier survives. The rules live in the
56	  routing table in [`EUDR_CROPS.md`](EUDR_CROPS.md) — one editable place shared
57	  with the EUDR scope queries, not duplicated in SQL:
58	
59	  | `mbmode24` | Keeps | Drops |
60	  |---|---|---|
61	  | Pasture (15), Mosaic of Uses (21) | `slaughter_point` | silo, catchment, mill |
62	  | Sugar cane (20) | `mill_point` | silo, catchment, slaughter |
63	  | Soybean (39), Other Temporary (41) | `intake_point`, catchment | slaughter, mill |
64	  | Agriculture (18) | `intake_point`, catchment, `mill_point` | slaughter |
65	  | Coffee (46), Palm Oil (35) | nothing | every delivery tier |
66	  | unknown / NULL | everything | — |
67	
68	  Class 18 is MapBiomas' generic agriculture parent and can itself *be* cane, so it
69	  deliberately keeps both grain and mill rather than guessing. Class 21 is a
70	  mixed-use mosaic assumed to be pasture, and that assumption is carried as a
71	  caveat on every number derived from it.
72	
73	  Coffee and palm keep **no** delivery candidate: they are real EUDR commodities,
74	  but the facilities product has no tier for either, so the cadaster gets its
75	  membership relationship and a reported `no_match`. Substituting a grain silo
76	  would name an organisation with no relationship to that farm.
77	- **Cross-border proximity override.** A delivery facility closer than
78	  `proximity_override_km` is promoted to the top and flagged `nearest_by_far`,
79	  while the relationship match is still shown. Delivery matching is **never gated
80	  on município** — a silo just across a municipal line competes on equal footing.
81	  Mills do not participate (see above).
82	
83	### Ties in the ranking
84	
85	The full order is: `nearest_by_far` promotions first, then the tier order
86	above, then `distance_km` ascending with catchment candidates (no distance)
87	last, then `evidence_value` descending. **Where two candidates are equal on all
88	of those, the lower `entity_id` ranks first.**
89	
90	Distance ties are ordinary, not exotic. On the Goiás sample list 45 cadasters
91	have two facilities at an identical distance, and for one of them the tie is
92	for the single nearest delivery point, which is the value q26 reports. Without
93	the `entity_id` rule those rankings fall to scan order, and the `max_candidates`

# Cadaster → cooperative / buyer candidate matching

This document is the **single source of truth** for how a cadaster on a list is
matched to the cooperative(s) and buyer(s) it should be *put in contact with*
about deforestation on its land. Like [`MATCHING.md`](MATCHING.md), it is written
so a human *or* an AI agent can change the policy by editing numbers in one place:
the build reads the thresholds from `lists.json` (the `coops` block, per-project
default) and passes them into `sql/list/coop_match.sql.tmpl` — so **changing a
rule = editing the config, not the SQL.**

## The decision, in one sentence

> Each cadaster gets a **ranked set of candidates** — never a single forced
> assignment. A wrong single match sends a trader to the wrong organisation about
> a named farmer's land; two candidates with evidence beat one confident guess.

## Two families of evidence, both surfaced, never collapsed

- **"Who has the relationship?"** — the cooperative that counts this farmer as a
  member. The influence lever. Matched **by município**.
- **"Where would they deliver?"** — the nearest silo (grain), slaughterhouse
  (cattle), or mill (sugar cane). The logistics lever. Matched **by distance**,
  município-agnostic.

Both are real levers; the report shows both and lets the human weigh them.

## The tiers (consumed from the `soft_commodity_infrastructure/` product)

| Tier | Answers | Entity | Basis | Match rule |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `membership_muni` | relationship | cooperative | observed | município code = cadaster's |
| `intake_point` | delivery (grain) | coop silo | observed | distance ≤ radius |
| `slaughter_point` | delivery (cattle) | **buyer** | observed | distance ≤ radius |
| `mill_point` | delivery (sugar cane) | **mill** | observed | distance ≤ radius |
| `gravity_catchment` | delivery | coop | **modelled** | cadaster in catchment |

`branch_footprint` and `hq_point` (RFB) arrive with Plan 1b. `slaughter_point` and
`mill_point` are **buyers**, not co-ops — flagged `entity_kind='buyer'` /
`'mill'` so the report never implies a membership relationship.

`mill_point` is ranked below the other two delivery tiers because ANP publishes no
street address for mills: each sits at its town's centroid, so its distance is
town-to-cadaster, not gate-to-cadaster. Every mill candidate carries the flag
`town_centroid`, and mills are **excluded from the proximity override** — a
centroid landing inside 10 km is an artefact of the geocode, not evidence.

## Ranking — observed relationship before modelled proximity

1. `membership_muni` → 2. `intake_point` / `slaughter_point` → 3. `mill_point` →
4. `gravity_catchment`

with two overrides:

- **Commodity routes the delivery tier.** The cadaster's dominant crop (Trazo
  `mbmode24`) selects which delivery tier survives. The rules live in the
  routing table in [`EUDR_CROPS.md`](EUDR_CROPS.md) — one editable place shared
  with the EUDR scope queries, not duplicated in SQL:

  | `mbmode24` | Keeps | Drops |
  |---|---|---|
  | Pasture (15), Mosaic of Uses (21) | `slaughter_point` | silo, catchment, mill |
  | Sugar cane (20) | `mill_point` | silo, catchment, slaughter |
  | Soybean (39), Other Temporary (41) | `intake_point`, catchment | slaughter, mill |
  | Agriculture (18) | `intake_point`, catchment, `mill_point` | slaughter |
  | Coffee (46), Palm Oil (35) | nothing | every delivery tier |
  | unknown / NULL | everything | — |

  Class 18 is MapBiomas' generic agriculture parent and can itself *be* cane, so it
  deliberately keeps both grain and mill rather than guessing. Class 21 is a
  mixed-use mosaic assumed to be pasture, and that assumption is carried as a
  caveat on every number derived from it.

  Coffee and palm keep **no** delivery candidate: they are real EUDR commodities,
  but the facilities product has no tier for either, so the cadaster gets its
  membership relationship and a reported `no_match`. Substituting a grain silo
  would name an organisation with no relationship to that farm.
- **Cross-border proximity override.** A delivery facility closer than
  `proximity_override_km` is promoted to the top and flagged `nearest_by_far`,
  while the relationship match is still shown. Delivery matching is **never gated
  on município** — a silo just across a municipal line competes on equal footing.
  Mills do not participate (see above).

### Ties in the ranking

The full order is: `nearest_by_far` promotions first, then the tier order
above, then `distance_km` ascending with catchment candidates (no distance)
last, then `evidence_value` descending. **Where two candidates are equal on all
of those, the lower `entity_id` ranks first.**

Distance ties are ordinary, not exotic. On the Goiás sample list 45 cadasters
have two facilities at an identical distance, and for one of them the tie is
for the single nearest delivery point, which is the value q26 reports. Without
the `entity_id` rule those rankings fall to scan order, and the `max_candidates`
cap then drops whichever candidate the query plan happened to plough last.

The same reasoning applies as in [`MATCHING.md`](MATCHING.md): the tie-break
does not have to be meaningful, but it does have to be written down, or two
correct implementations disagree. Unlike the containment fractions there, these
distances carry no tolerance — a `distance_km` computed a slightly different
way can still order two near-equal facilities either way.

## Widening — target a count, not a radius

If fewer than `min_candidates` delivery candidates fall within `intake_km`, widen
the radius toward `intake_km_ceiling` until the count is met. When widening
happened, mark `widened`; when even the ceiling yields none, mark `no_match` — a
match failure is **reported, never hidden** (see `l09`). Measured rationale: on
the Goiás sample the nearest cooperative silo to Jussara is 58 km and a fixed
100 km radius returns a single operator, which violates "give people options";
widening to a count is what actually serves the user.

## Parameters (defaults; override per list in `lists.json → coops`)

| Parameter | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `max_candidates` | 5 | cap on listed candidates per cadaster |
| `min_candidates` | 2 | widen until this many delivery candidates exist |
| `intake_km` | 100 | initial delivery radius (58 km is *not* far for rural Brazil — widening is expected, not failure) |
| `intake_km_ceiling` | 300 | hard stop; beyond this, report `no_match` |
| `proximity_override_km` | 10 | a delivery point closer than this is surfaced first (`nearest_by_far`) |
| `gravity_decay` | 2.0 | distance exponent for the modelled catchment |
| `min_capacity_t` | 1000 | ignore trivial storage units — **gates `intake_point` only**, since slaughter capacity is a band and mill capacity is m³/day, neither of them tonnes |

Distances are computed in **EPSG:5880** (SIRGAS 2000 Brazil Polyconic), *not* in
degrees — unlike the areal ratios in `MATCHING.md`, which are CRS-cancelling.

They run from the **cadastral parcel's centroid** to the facility point. A large
property spans several kilometres, so measuring from its centroid and measuring
from its nearest boundary give materially different answers, and every ranking
threshold here — `intake_km`, `intake_km_ceiling`, `proximity_override_km` — is
read against the centroid figure.

## What each candidate carries forward

For every candidate the match records, so the report and any reviewer can see
*why* it was surfaced:

- `tier`, `basis` (observed | modelled), `entity_kind` (cooperative | buyer)
- `distance_km` (delivery tiers), `evidence_value` (membership count / capacity)
- `rank` and any `flags` (`widened`, `no_match`, `nearest_by_far`)

Cadasters and the candidates considered-and-rejected are counted in
`l09_coop_reconciliation.sql` so nothing is silently dropped — the same
auditable-exclusion discipline as `l07`.

The cap is applied before that count: ranking runs over every candidate, the
top `max_candidates` per cadaster are kept, and reconciliation counts what was
kept. So `n_candidates` never exceeds `max_candidates`, and a cadaster with
forty candidates in range reports five. Ranking decides which five, which is
what the tier order and the `nearest_by_far` promotion are for.

# Question set: EUDR workflow benchmark, 30 questions across 6 dependent stages.
#
# The agent receives this file, prompts/task.md, the policy documents in
# policies/, and the input list. Golden fixtures are generated by the vendored
# rural-land SQL (oracle/render.py) and are NEVER mounted into a session.
#
# Each question declares:
#   stage       1-6, the workflow stage it belongs to
#   depends_on  question ids whose result it builds on (may be empty)
# so the grader can separate a question wrong on its own merits from one wrong
# because an upstream answer was wrong (harness/grade.py stage_summary).
#
# Output contracts specify columns by MEANING and TYPE. The grader is
# column-name- and column-order-insensitive and compares rows as a multiset.
# Column names in the answer CSV are the agent's choice; meanings are not.
# rows: null means the row count is data-determined; the grader takes it from
# the golden file.
#
# grading: geometry marks questions whose numbers move under reasonable method
# choices (equal-area projection, spherical vs ellipsoidal distance). Those
# grade at relative 1e-2 with integer slack max(2, 1% of golden); everything
# else at relative 1e-3.
#
# Every question reporting an absolute area or distance carries it, because no
# convention for either is stated anywhere and none should be: the oracle
# computes hectares on the WGS84 spheroid only because this Trazo3 release
# ships no area column, which is an accident of the source data rather than a
# rule worth imposing. Geodesic area, an equal-area projection, and Brazil
# Polyconic land within a percent of each other, so the tolerance covers the
# spread and the session picks its own method.
#
# q23 is the exception, and grades strict despite reporting hectares. Integer
# slack would apply to its field_id as well, since the grader tries column
# permutations and cannot tell an identifier from a quantity. Neighbouring
# plots carry adjacent ids, so the slack would credit an answer naming the
# wrong farm — a worse failure than rejecting a valid area method.
#
# Deforestation comes from the era-band columns only; hansen_covered_area is
# never used. Which land-cover classes fall under the regulation is governed by
# policies/EUDR_CROPS.md, which the agent is given — the task is to APPLY that
# policy correctly across the workflow, not to guess it.

cat > /tmp/init.sql <<'EOF'
INSTALL spatial; LOAD spatial; INSTALL httpfs; LOAD httpfs;
SET enable_progress_bar=false; SET memory_limit='12GB'; SET geometry_always_xy=true;
EOF
time duckdb /tmp/work.db -init /tmp/init.sql -box -c "
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE parcels_union AS SELECT ST_Union_Agg(geom) AS u FROM parcels;
-- all intersecting field-parcel pairs
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE fp AS
SELECT f.field_id, p.cod_imovel,
       ST_Area(f.geom) AS field_area_deg,
       ST_Area(ST_Intersection(f.geom, p.geom)) AS inter_deg
FROM fields_env f JOIN parcels p ON ST_Intersects(f.geom, p.geom);
-- per-field single best fraction
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE field_single AS
SELECT field_id, field_area_deg,
       max(inter_deg/field_area_deg) AS best_single_frac,
       arg_max(cod_imovel, inter_deg) AS dom_parcel
FROM fp GROUP BY field_id, field_area_deg;
-- per-field union fraction
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE field_union AS
SELECT f.field_id,
       ST_Area(ST_Intersection(f.geom, u.u))/ST_Area(f.geom) AS union_frac
FROM fields_env f, parcels_union u
WHERE ST_Intersects(f.geom, u.u);
SELECT count(*) pairs FROM fp;
SELECT count(*) fields_intersecting FROM field_single;
" 2>&1 | tail -12

cat > /tmp/init.sql <<'EOF'
INSTALL spatial; LOAD spatial; INSTALL httpfs; LOAD httpfs;
SET enable_progress_bar=false; SET memory_limit='12GB'; SET geometry_always_xy=true;
EOF
duckdb /tmp/work.db -init /tmp/init.sql -box -c "
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE field_match AS
SELECT s.field_id, s.dom_parcel, s.best_single_frac,
       coalesce(u.union_frac,0) AS union_frac,
       (s.best_single_frac>=0.5) AS single_ok,
       (coalesce(u.union_frac,0)>=0.5) AS union_ok
FROM field_single s LEFT JOIN field_union u USING(field_id);
SELECT
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE single_ok OR union_ok) AS matched,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE single_ok) AS by_single,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE union_ok AND NOT single_ok) AS by_agg_only,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE NOT single_ok AND NOT union_ok) AS excluded
FROM field_match;
"

SELECT fm.field_id, fm.dom_parcel AS cod_imovel, p.municipio,

       fe.e0104/1e4 e0104_ha, fe.e0509/1e4 e0509_ha, fe.e1014/1e4 e1014_ha,

  CASE WHEN d.dominant_mb IN (15,21) THEN 'slaughter_point'
       WHEN d.dominant_mb IN (39,41) THEN 'intake_point'
       WHEN d.dominant_mb=20 THEN 'mill_point'

  f.inscope_post2020
FROM flagged f JOIN dom d USING(cod_imovel);
-- all delivery candidates (routed tier) with distance, capacity gate for intake
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE delcand AS
SELECT r.cod_imovel, f.entity_id, f.tier, f.entity_kind, f.weight, f.basis, f.geom_method,
       ST_Distance(c.c5880, f.p5880)/1000 AS dist_km
FROM froute r
JOIN cen c ON c.cod_imovel=r.cod_imovel
JOIN fac f ON f.tier=r.del_tier
WHERE (f.tier<>'intake_point' OR f.weight>=1000);
-- summary per cadaster
SELECT r.del_tier, count(*) FROM froute r GROUP BY 1;
SELECT r.cod_imovel, r.del_tier,
   min(d.dist_km) nearest_km,
   count(*) FILTER(WHERE d.dist_km<=100) within100,
   count(*) FILTER(WHERE d.dist_km<10) within10
FROM froute r JOIN delcand d USING(cod_imovel)

All 30 question answers plus `workflow.csv` are written to `answers/`. Here's what I did and the key results.

## Approach
- Read all three policy docs + `questions.yaml`, then queried the three GeoParquet datasets with DuckDB (`spatial`+`httpfs`). I pulled the 117 listed parcels out of the 8.45M-row CAR file remotely, and cached the Goiás field file (772k rows) and facilities file locally for the repeated spatial work.
- **Areas**: hectares via `ST_Area_Spheroid` on WGS84 with `geometry_always_xy=true` (verified it reconciles with the file's own `mbcov_area_2024`). **Distances**: parcel-centroid→facility in EPSG:5880, km. **Post-2020 loss** = the `deforestarea2124` era band only.

## Headline findings
- **Input list**: 117 IDs, all resolve cleanly in CAR — no duplicates, no missing, none <1 ha (a clean `csv` encoding).
- **Matching**: 872 fields intersect a listed parcel → **798 matched** (788 single-parcel, 10 aggregate-only), 74 excluded; 37,144 ha total.
- **EUDR classes present**: Pasture(15)+Mosaic(21)=cattle, Soybean(39)=soya (in scope); Other Temporary Crops(41) excluded. Post-2020 loss on in-scope crops: cattle 67.9 ha, soya 52.6 ha.
- **Portfolio decision**: **19 cadasters non-compliant** (post-2020 loss on cattle/soya). Top contact is the município cooperative (`membership_muni`) for 17, and a nearby slaughterhouse buyer (proximity override <10 km) for 2. No widening, no no-match cases.

## One important caveat
The policy files (`COOPS.md`, `EUDR_CROPS.md`) repeatedly cite a **`MATCHING.md`** for the field-to-cadaster containment rules, but that file is **not present** in `policies/` (only INPUTS/EUDR_CROPS/COOPS are). Stage-3 questions (Q9–Q14, and everything downstream) depend on it. I implemented the standard interpretation the question text implies:
- **single-parcel rule**: a field is admitted if ≥ 50% of its area lies in one listed parcel;
- **whole-list aggregate rule**: admitted if ≥ 50% lies in the union of all listed parcels (catches boundary-straddling fields);
- containment fractions computed as CRS-cancelling areal ratios; each field assigned to its dominant (largest-overlap) parcel.

If `MATCHING.md` specified a different threshold, the Stage-3+ counts would shift accordingly — that's the only place my numbers rest on an inferred rule rather than a stated one.
